# How to Become a Source the LLMs Trust

<callout icon="◈" color="blue_bg">
	**Claim boundary.** No page can make an LLM, search engine, or retrieval system trust, cite, or represent a source in a particular way. This draft covers practices that make a public source easier to identify, inspect, and maintain.
</callout>

## The practical goal

The useful question is not whether a model trusts a site. The useful question is whether a person can identify the source, inspect its claim, trace its evidence, understand its scope, and revisit it after the context changes.

Google describes helpful, reliable, people-first content as material that provides original information, reporting, research, or analysis; adds value beyond rewriting; shows clear sourcing; and makes authorship understandable. [Google guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)

For Google AI features, existing SEO practices remain relevant, and Google states that there are no additional requirements or special optimizations to appear. A page must be eligible for Search, but eligibility does not guarantee crawling, indexing, retrieval, linking, or citation. [Google AI features guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)

## The source record

### 1. Identity

State who is speaking. Use a stable name, a clear author or organization page, and a truthful account of what the source can responsibly address.

### 2. Evidence

Show what supports the claim. Link primary material when available. Distinguish first-hand observation, calculation, interpretation, and opinion.

### 3. Access

Put the useful answer in the readable main content. Use a descriptive title, stable URL, clear headings, and links to the definitions and methods that give the page context.

### 4. Maintenance

Show a review cue, preserve sources, name unresolved questions, and correct the record when evidence changes. A source record is a practice, not a one-time asset.

## What makes the work non-commodity

Google's generative-search guidance distinguishes unique, expert-led, or first-hand material from content that mainly restates what is already available. It also cautions against creating pages solely for query variation or pursuing inauthentic mentions. [Google generative AI optimization guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide)

For this site, the applied standard is simple: make the signal legible. A framework should label itself as a working framework rather than an external standard. An answer-engine observation should include platform, query, date, capture, source links, and limits. A systems claim should name dependencies and decision ownership.

## Technical legibility

Technical clarity is access, not proof. Google recommends keeping important content in text, using internal links, providing a good page experience, and ensuring structured data matches visible content. [Google AI features guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)

Structured data can provide explicit clues about a page's meaning and support eligible Search appearances. It should describe visible page content; it is not a citation switch, and blank pages should not exist only to hold markup. [Google structured data documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/intro-structured-data)

## Working sequence

1. Choose one consequential reader question.
2. Write the direct answer in the main body.
3. Build the evidence trail, including dates and claim limits.
4. Link the page to the relevant definitions and methods.
5. Review the record separately from any platform-specific observation.
